topicTitle: Lists of Data: Arrays & Index Operations

lessons.title: Creating Arrays & Zero-Indexed Access
lessons.description: Learn how to create arrays — ordered collections of values — and access items using their position number (index).

sections.heading: What is an array?
paragraphs: An array is a list-like data structure that holds multiple values in a single variable. Think of it as a row of boxes, each with a numbered slot. Arrays can store any combination of types — numbers, strings, booleans, even other arrays.

sections.heading: Creating arrays
paragraphs: You create an array using square brackets []. Separate each item with a comma. You can also use the Array() constructor, but the literal syntax [] is more common and preferred.

sections.heading: Zero-based indexing
paragraphs: Array positions start at 0, not 1. The first element is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on. This is called zero-based indexing and is one of the most important concepts for beginners to grasp.

codeExamples.heading: Creating and accessing arrays
codeExamples.code:
let fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];

console.log(fruits[0]);  // "apple"
console.log(fruits[1]);  // "banana"
console.log(fruits[2]);  // "cherry"
console.log(fruits.length);  // 3
explanation: The array fruits holds three string values.
Indices start at 0, so fruits[0] gives the first item, not fruits[1].
.length tells you how many items are in the array.

codeExamples.heading: Mixed types and out-of-bounds access
codeExamples.code:
let mixed = [42, "hello", true, null];

console.log(mixed[0]);  // 42
console.log(mixed[2]);  // true

console.log(mixed[10]); // undefined (no error!)
explanation: Arrays can hold different types — numbers, strings, booleans, null.
Accessing an index that doesn't exist returns undefined instead of throwing an error.
This is different from many other languages, which would throw an error for out-of-bounds access.
codeExamples.output:
> console.log(mixed[0]);  // 42
> console.log(mixed[2]);  // true
> console.log(mixed[10]); // undefined (no error!)
42
true
undefined (no error!)

practice.task: Create an array of your three favorite movies. Log the second movie using its index. Then log the total number of movies using .length.
hints: Access the second movie with movies[1] (remember, indices start at 0!)
practice.note: Try accessing movies[3] — what does it return?

keyTakeaways: Arrays store multiple values in a single variable using square brackets [].
Indices start at 0, not 1 — arr[0] is the first element.
Accessing a nonexistent index returns undefined, not an error.
lessons.challenge: Create an array of 5 numbers. Write a loop that prints each number along with its index, like: Index 0: 10, Index 1: 20, etc.

lessons.title: Adding/Removing Elements (push, pop, shift, unshift)
lessons.description: Master the four fundamental methods for adding and removing items from the beginning or end of an array.

sections.heading: Four essential array methods
paragraphs: Arrays are dynamic — you can add or remove elements at any time. JavaScript gives you four core methods that modify arrays in place:
list: push() — adds to the end of the array
pop() — removes from the end of the array
unshift() — adds to the beginning of the array
shift() — removes from the beginning of the array

sections.heading: Return values
paragraphs: push() and unshift() return the new length of the array. pop() and shift() return the removed element. Knowing these return values helps you chain operations or store results.

codeExamples.heading: push and pop — working from the end
explanation: push(40) adds 40 to the end of the array.
pop() removes and returns the last element (40).
The array is modified in place — the original variable changes.

codeExamples.heading: shift and unshift — working from the front
explanation: unshift("z") adds "z" to the beginning, shifting everything else right.
shift() removes and returns the first element ("z").
These are the mirror operations of push and pop, but at the front.

practice.task: Create an empty array called todoList. Use push() to add three tasks. Then use pop() to remove one. Finally, use unshift() to add an urgent task to the front.
hints: Remove: todoList.pop() — it returns the removed task.
practice.note: Try chaining: console.log(todoList.push("new")) — what does it return?

keyTakeaways: push() adds to the end; pop() removes from the end.
unshift() adds to the beginning; shift() removes from the beginning.
All four methods modify the array in place and return useful values.
lessons.challenge: Simulate a playlist: start with ["Song A", "Song B"]. Add "Song C" to the end, add "Song Z" to the front, remove the last song, then remove the first song. Print the array after each operation.

lessons.title: Splicing & Slicing Arrays (splice, slice)
lessons.description: Learn the difference between splice (which modifies the original array) and slice (which creates a copy) — two essential but easily confused methods.

sections.heading: slice — creates a copy
paragraphs: slice() extracts a portion of an array into a new array without changing the original. It takes two arguments: a start index and an optional end index (exclusive).

sections.heading: splice — modifies in place
paragraphs: splice() changes the original array by removing, replacing, or adding elements. It takes a start index, an optional delete count, and optional items to insert. It returns an array of removed elements.

sections.heading: Key difference
list: Use slice() when you want to preserve the original
Use splice() when you intentionally want to change the array

codeExamples.heading: slice — extracting without modifying
explanation: slice(1, 3) copies elements at index 1 and 2 (not 3 — the end is exclusive).
The original colors array remains completely unchanged.
Omitting the end index slices from start to the end of the array.

codeExamples.heading: splice — modifying the original
explanation: splice(1, 2) removes 2 elements starting at index 1 and returns them.
The original array is modified — "b" and "c" are gone.
splice(1, 0, "x", "y") inserts "x" and "y" at index 1 without removing anything.

practice.task: Given let nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], use slice() to get [20, 30, 40] and store it in a new variable. Then use splice() to remove the first element from the original array. Log both arrays.
practice.note: Always double-check: did you mean slice (copy) or splice (modify)?

keyTakeaways: slice(start, end) copies a portion into a new array — the original stays unchanged.
splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) modifies the original array in place.
The end index in slice() is exclusive — it stops before that position.
If you want to keep the original array, use slice(); if you want to change it, use splice().
lessons.challenge: Given let data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], use slice() to create three separate copies: one with the first half, one with the second half, and one with just the middle two elements. Then use splice() to remove all even numbers from the original.

lessons.title: Array Destructuring & Spread Operator Syntax (...)
lessons.description: Use modern ES6+ syntax to unpack arrays into variables and merge arrays effortlessly — cleaner, shorter, and more expressive code.

sections.heading: Array destructuring
paragraphs: Destructuring lets you unpack array values into individual variables in one line. Instead of accessing each element by index, you assign them all at once using the same square bracket syntax.

sections.heading: The spread operator (...)
paragraphs: The spread operator ... expands an array into its individual elements. It's useful for copying arrays, merging arrays, and passing elements as function arguments.

sections.heading: Common patterns
list: const [a, b] = arr; — unpack first two elements
const [first, ...rest] = arr; — first element + everything else as a new array
const [...copy] = arr; — shallow copy of an array

codeExamples.heading: Destructuring in action
explanation: Destructuring assigns each element to a variable by position.
You can skip elements by leaving the position empty between commas.
This is much cleaner than writing let red = rgb[0]; for each one.

codeExamples.heading: Spread operator for copying and merging
explanation: [...arr1] expands arr1 into individual elements, creating a shallow copy.
Spreading multiple arrays combines them into one — cleaner than concat().
You can mix spread elements with individual values in the same array literal.

practice.task: Given let scores = [85, 92, 78, 95, 88], use destructuring to get the first and last scores into separate variables. Then use spread to create a new array that has all scores plus a new score of 100 at the end.
hints: Destructure: let [first, , , , last] = scores; or use scores[0] and scores[scores.length - 1].
practice.note: Destructuring also works with objects (covered in topic 2.6) — the syntax is similar but uses {}.

keyTakeaways: Array destructuring unpacks values into variables: const [a, b] = arr;
Use commas to skip positions: const [first, , third] = arr;
The spread operator ... expands arrays for copying ([...arr]) or merging ([...a, ...b]).
Both features make code shorter, cleaner, and easier to read.
lessons.challenge: Write a function getMinMax(arr) that uses destructuring with Math.min() and Math.max() to return an object with the smallest and largest values. Test with [5, 2, 8, 1, 9].
